messages.subject: Re: Bootstrapping with autocorrelated data
messages.body_plain:
Dear Bevan,

As you noticed it is not possible to bootstrap something which is not
i.i.d.  I would look for an appropriate ARMA-model and then simulate new
series using this model (functions arima.mle, arima.diag, and arima.sim).
"Real" bootstrapping would probably sample the residuals to obtain
innovations - I would check for Normality and then probably just use the
estimated SD as input to arima.sim.

Regards,
Henrik

messages.subject: Re: ordering rows in dotplot
messages.body_plain:
David Parkhurst wrote:
> I have a dataframe consisting of three columns:  an ordered factor named
> f.ord, a numeric variable x, and a second factor f2.  When I ask for
> dotplot(f.ord ~ x | f2), the plots come out with the f.ord rows ordered
> alphabetically, rather than in the order I specified.  How can I
> control the sequence at which they are plotted.  I thought that would
> be one of the purposes of  "ordered".
> Dave Parkhurst

It is. Try:

dF <- data.frame(x = rnorm(100),
                 f1 = ordered(rep(1:5, 20), c(1, 4, 3, 2, 5)),
                 f2 = factor(rep(letters[1:5], each = 20)))
dotplot(f1 ~ x | f2, dF)

# now try a different ordering
levels(dF$f1) <- c(5, 3, 4, 1, 2)
dotplot(f1 ~ x | f2, dF)

I'm using S-PLUS 6.1 on Windows 2000. This example also works as 
expected in R-1.8.0.

-sundar

messages.subject: Re: cv.tree
messages.body_plain:
You 
should worry if you always get the same answer from different runs of CV.  
Cross-validation *randomly* divide the data up into training and test sets 
multiple times.  In different runs of CV, you should expect different 
partitioning of the data into training and test sets.  If you always see 
the same result, it's pretty good evidence that the program is using the same 
partitioning every time, probably because the same seed for random number 
generator is used every time.

 

I 
seem to recall that CART has an option somewhere that lets you set the random 
seed.  I can't check because I don't have the software.

 

Andy

messages.subject: Re: source of computation errors
messages.body_plain:
On Tue, 2003-11-04 at 14:06, Carlos Carroll wrote:
> Can someone suggest a reason for these small errors in simple
> arithmetic
> computations in S-Plus (v. Pro 6.0.3 Release 2, Windows 2000)?
> Hopefully, this isn't too much of a newbie question. Is there
> something in
> the options() that is set incorrectly?
> 
> > 6.0859-.6053
> [1] 5.4805999999999999
> 
> > 16.0859+9.6053
> [1] 25.691199999999998
> 
> > 86.0859-79.6053
> [1] 6.4805999999999955

You might want to check:

options("digits")

to see what it shows. The default is typically 7, which in the above
examples should result in:

> 6.0859 - .6053
[1] 5.4806
> 16.0859 + 9.6053
[1] 25.6912
> 86.0859 - 79.6053
[1] 6.4806

However, if the default setting for 'digits' has been changed, to say
20:

> options(digits = 20)
> 6.0859 - .6053
[1] 5.4805999999999999
> 16.0859 + 9.6053
[1] 25.691199999999998
> 86.0859 - 79.6053
[1] 6.4805999999999955

The difference in the two being the number of significant digits shown
in the output.

The source of this "error"?

The IEEE 754 floating point representation standard.

Try this:

0.5 - 0.4 - 0.1

Should be 0 (zero) right?  Wrong.

In R (I don't have access to S-Plus), you get:

> 0.5 - 0.4 - 0.1
[1] -2.775558e-17

Internally, these numbers are stored in ways that cannot be exactly
represented. Thus, there will be rounding errors as a result and you see
this in the output.

For more information, you might want to go here:

http://grouper.ieee.org/groups/754/

You might also want to read:

What Every Computer Scientist Should Know about Floating-Point
Arithmetic, by David Goldberg. There is a link on the above page for it.

HTH,

Marc Schwartz

messages.subject: Re: Urgent:Putting legends on timeseries plots
messages.body_plain:
The plot method for timeSeries objects, plot.timeSeries, works a bit
differently than the other plot methods. To specify line types, colors etc
you must use the plot.args() argument. For example, to set the line type and
color for a plot of three series in the timeSeries object my.timeSeries use

Plot(my.timeSeries,plot.args(lty=c(1,2,3),col=c(1,2,3)))

You can add a legend using the legend command. 

Legend(0,10,legend=c("series 1","series 2", "series 3"),
lty=c(1,2,3), col=c(1,2,3)))

the x-axis location of the legend is specified by a number between 0 and 1,
indicating the percentage of the x-axis to locate the left corner of the
legeng. The y-axis location is specified in units of the data being plotted.
In the example above, the x-y co-ordinates are (0,10). This puts the legend
in the left corner of the plot, with the top left corner of the of the
legend at the point (0,10). It is best to display the plot first to see
where you want the legend to go and then issue the legend command. 

ez

I would need to fit the power function:

y = c*x^z

with maximum likelihood estimates of parameters 'c' and 'z'. Assuming a
log-normal distribution, how can I implement it?

Many thanks in advance,

LV
messages.body_snippet:
I would need to fit the power function:

y = c*x^z

with maximum likelihood estimates of parameters 'c' and 'z'. Assuming a
log-normal distribution, how can I implement it?

Many thanks in advance,

L

messages.subject: Re: MLE for power function
messages.body_plain:
Have you considered the following: 

     log(y) = log(c) + z*log(z)  + error

     In this form, estimating log(c) and z would just be ordinary least 
squares, which you can do with "lm".  If a substantial portion of your 
"y's" are 0 or negative, you can't do this. 

     The standard least squares assumptions require the error to be 
approximately normally distributed with constant variance.  If you are 
dealing with money or with many physical measurements, taking logarithms 
is standard in many cases and makes more sense than the form you wrote.  
I would do this first and then do a normal probability plot (qqnorm) of 
the residuals to help decide if I should do more. 

     If the residuals looked strange or I needed to fit y = c*x^z for 
other reasons, then I'd try "nls" or "optim" in the MASS library, 
possibly using the numbers I got from "lm" for starting values. 

     hope this helps.  spencer graves

messages.subject: Re: MLE for power function
messages.body_plain:
You have to be careful with log transforms, however, since (depending on
whether your errors come in multiplicatively or additively), you can get
biased parameters this way.  For this reason, the nls or optim suggestions
may be preferable.

Examples of problems with log transforms distorting data are given in Zhou,
X.-H., S. Gao, et al. (1997). "Methods for comparing the means of two
log-normal samples." Biometrics 53: 1129-1135, Parkhurst, D. F. (1998).
"Arithmetic versus geometric means for environmental concentration data."
Environmental Science and Technology 32(3): 92A-98A, and Fisher, L. D. and
G. van Belle (1993). Biostatistics. A Methodology for the Health Sciences.
(p. 466) New York, John Wiley & Sons, Inc.

Dave Parkhurst

messages.subject: dividind data from a very long time series
messages.subject_clean: dividind data from a very long time series
messages.body_plain:
My timeseries of daily data is composed by a dataframe of two columns;
in the first column the date is dd/mm/yyyy, which in my case is not defined as
dates but 
as character;
in the second column there are the data.
This time series is quite long, more than two centuries.

I know that
tapply(mydataframe[[2]], unpaste(mydataframe[[1]], sep = "/") , c)
will divide my data year by year, and for each year there will be a matrix
with 12 columns (one for each month) and 31 rows (one for each day);
tapply(mydataframe[[2]], unpaste(mydataframe[[1]], sep = "/")[[1]] , c)
will divide my data by days (the first day of each month for all the years,
the second day of each month for all the years, ...)
tapply(mydataframe[[2]], unpaste(mydataframe[[1]], sep = "/")[[2]] , c)
will divide my data by months (the first month of each year for all the years,
the second month of each year for all the years, ...)

I need to take all the 1st of January for a given lag (e.g. 1961-1990); then
all the 2nd of January and so on until the 31th of December.
I am able to do that using quite a certain number of loops, but I was
wondering whether there is a more direct and faster way of doing that (with a
correct use of tapply for example).

thank you for your help
Stefano

If you're using S-PLUS 6.1 (you never said), then try using timeDate 
objects:

# let `y' be data.frame with your date in column "time"
y$time <- timeDate(y$time, "%m/%d/%Y")
# now subset by month/day/Year
y[months(y$time) == "Feb" & days(y$time) == 29 &
  (years(y$time) > 1961 & years(y$time) < 1991), ]

Hope this is what you need,

Sundar

messages.body_plain:
Dear Splus users:

I am using nlminb to maximize a pretty complicated likelihood. I generate data
from a known distribution and minimize -log-likelihood to check that the
parameter values I used to generate the data are returned to me.

After running several simulations, the parameter estimates look great (very
close to true parameters with p>.10 for all parameters) but there are error

messages or what I can do to solve the problem of the singularity?

Suzanne Szwarc

messages.body_plain:
Hi, all,

I have question for the following double integration function. The first double integration works, but I want to generalize it so that I can do the more general double integration, so I tried to write second function, but it does not work, I can not figure out why, Anyone can help me out?  The sample code that performs similar double integration will be helpful.

  thanks in advance,

  Steve

double.demo <- function()
{
        fun <- function(y)
        unlist(lapply(y, function(y)
        {
                integrate(f=function(x, y)
 x+y,
                lower=1-y,
                upper=y,
                y=y)$integral
        }))
        integrate(f=fun, lower=0.5, upper=1)$integral
}

double.demo()

double.demo2 <- function(aa)
{
        fun <- function(y, aa)
        unlist(lapply(y, function(y, aa=aa)
 
        {
                integrate(f=function(x, y, aa=aa) aa*x+y,
                lower=1-y,
                upper=y,
                y=y, aa=aa)$integral
        }))
        integrate(f=fun, lower=0.5, upper=1, aa=aa)$integral
}

double.demo2(2)

On Mon, 10 Nov 2003, Erin Hodgess wrote:

> Dear S People:
> 
> I'm trying to put together a FORTRAN subroutine to work with S code.
> 
> 
> I (finally) figured out createChapter and I created S.dll
> 
> Then I open the dll via
> dyn.open("S.dll")

S.dll is automatically loaded when a chapter is opened.

> When I run the s function, I get the error message that the
> subroutinne is not in the load table.
>

Is your subroutine actually exported by S.dll (by default nothing is 
exported in many compiler systems)?

If so, is the name mangling the same?

The way I would answer both questions is to run pedump -e S.dll and list 
the exports.  pedump.exe is found in many places, one being in
http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/Rtools/tools.zip.

As far as I know on Windows S-PLUS just appends _ to the symbol, and does 
not change the case.  So the symbol shown by pedump should be the same as 
that called by .Fortran except for an appended _ .

It will still depend on how much data you have (that is,

how noisy your estimate is) and what you want to do

(which I might be able to guess).

I have some data on 200 US stocks hanging about.

These are picked sort of at random -- there are some

large cap stocks and some small stocks -- so their

distribution of correlations is probably lower than those

from a typical index.  The 95th percentile correlation

is 0.33, 98th is 0.40, 99th is 0.46 and the max is 0.83.

Another thing to keep in mind is that correlations of

returns change significantly over time, which is going to

affect your estimates and how you should think about

them.

We are happy to announce that the first R user conference

  useR! 2004

is scheduled for May 20-22 2004 and will take place at the Vienna
University of Technology.

The conference will focus on
  - giving an overview of the new features of the rapidly
    evolving R project,
  - providing a platform for R users to discuss and exchange
    ideas how R can be used to do statistical computations,
    data analysis, visualization and exciting applications in
    various fields.

KEYNOTE LECTURES
A huge amount of exciting features and innovations came up in the last 
releases of R. How these features can be used efficiently will be 
presented in keynote lectures given by R core team members, addressing 
hot topics such as
  - grid Graphics
  - Good Programming Practice
  - Dynamic Documents
  - Language Interfaces
  - Packaging and Quality Assurance
  - Datamining and Large Databases

Speakers will include Peter Dalgaard, Kurt Hornik, Fritz Leisch, Paul 
Murrell and Brian D. Ripley.

USER-CONTRIBUTED SESSIONS
Oral and poster presentations will be a platform to bring together R 
users, contributers, package maintainers and developers in the S 
spirit that `users are developers'. People from different fields will 
show us how they solve problems with R in fascinating applications.

including Axel Benner, Roger Bivand, Dirk Eddelbuettel, John Fox, Kurt 
Hornik, Stefano Iacus, Steffen L. Lauritzen, Friedrich Leisch, Uwe 
Ligges and Martin Theus, and will cover topics such as
  - Finance & Econometrics
  - Visualization & Graphics
  - Spatial Statistics
  - Biostatistics
  - Graphical Models
  - and many more.

After the official presentations, Vienna's famous wine and beer pubs, 
cafes and restaurants proofed to be a very stimulating environment for 
fruitful discussions at previous meetings of the R community like this 
year's DSC 2003.

We invite all R users to submit abstracts on topics presenting 
innovations or exciting applications of R. A web page offering more 
information on the `useR!' conference, abstract submission, 
registration and Vienna is available at

messages.subject: Re: how to simulate the triangular distribution?
messages.subject_clean: how to simulate the triangular distribution?
messages.body_plain:
You 
need to find the quantile function of this triangular distribution, which you 
can do by writing down the density (straight line with y-intercept at 1/750 and 
slope -1/(750*1500)), integrate that to get the distribution function, and 
invert that to get the quantile function.  Then you can feed random 
uniform(0,1) into the quantile function to simulate from the triangular 
distribution.  (This is the probability integral 
transform.)

 

HTH,

Andy

messages.subject: User-defined covariance matrix
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am having problems locating help for creating my own covariance structures for residuals when fitting a GLS model.  

My data is made up of 100 individuals that have measurements recorded at four different time points.  So far the assumption has been made that the errors for measurements within individuals have an AR(1) relationship.  And that individuals are uncorrelated.  I've done this by using corr = corAR1(, form =  ~ 1 |id)) in the gls function and I am happy with the results.

However, it is believed that the measurements between individuals are also correlated.  The structure to be used now is the same as above if the measurements are from the same individual but if the measurements are from different individuals then the correlation is what it is above multiplied by some scalar (between 0 and 1).

I guess what I am asking is how can I create a covariance matrix that along the blocks on the diagonal follows R=AR(1) and for the off-diagonal blocks is a*R (where a is some scalar).

Regards

Mark

messages.subject: Re: Poisson regression in modeling survival data
messages.subject_clean: Poisson regression in modeling survival data
messages.body_plain:
You have not told us what you are trying to accomplish, which makes it
harder to give an answer.  But I can think of 2 things.

 1. To look at non-linear age effects.  In this case, it's easiest to
just use coxph
        fit <- coxph(Surv(futime,event) ~ pspline(age), data=m)
        plot(m$age, predict(fit))

It would be nice if coxph could have used the s(age) notation, but the s()
function is too closely tied to gam models.

2. Test for observed vs expected.  This is one thing addressed in the book,
where the Cox model determining "expected" survival comes from one data
set, often a large one, and we want to compare new data to it.
  This doesn't make a lot of sense when the "new" data is the same as the old.
  
  One issue that arises in this case is that the predicted for a Cox model
will have, like the Nelson-Aalen est, a value of 0 up until the first death.
>From your explanation, this appears to be at around time=70.  At any
time before then, the expected number of events is 0.  When one uses
gam or glm, the general form is y ~ x1 + x2 + ... + log(expected).  
If both y and expected are 0, this is fine from a loglik point of view,
but the glm code has trouble with one of the term 0 * log(0) that
arises in the computation.  (We know from L'Hopital's rule that this is 0,
but the computer doesn't).  You need to remove these data points from the
gam fit.  Since they add 0 to the loglik, independent of the x's, results
are correct with them gone.
   
        Terry Therneau

messages.subject: integrate
messages.body_plain:
Dear S+ users, 

I am grateful to all who answered my question, particularly to Petr
Pikal who  provided men with following two functions for  calculating
area under a curve:

"

In the firs one the 
limits are set from a plot in the second you have to state them 
explicitely. 

It is tested on R but you shall not have problems to translate it to 
S+
integ<-function (x,y)
{
replot(x,y)
meze<-locator(2)
dm<-meze$x[1]
hm<-meze$x[2]
abline(v=c(dm,hm),col=2)
vyber<-x<=hm&x>=dm
l<-length(x[vyber])
v<-diff(x[vyber])
z<-y[vyber][1:l-1]+y[vyber][2:l]
o<-z*v/2
osum<-sum(o)
o1<-
(y[x==min(x[vyber])]+y[x==max(x[vyber])])*(max(x[vyber])-
min(x[vyber]))/2
cista<-osum-o1
return(c(osum,cista))
}

integ1<-function (x,y,dm=-Inf,hm=+Inf)
{
if(dm==-Inf)dm<-min(x)
if(hm==+Inf)hm<-max(x)
vyber<-x<=hm&x>=dm
l<-length(x[vyber])
v<-diff(x[vyber])
z<-y[vyber][1:l-1]+y[vyber][2:l]
o<-z*v/2
osum<-sum(o)
o1<-
(y[x==min(x[vyber])]+y[x==max(x[vyber])])*(max(x[vyber])-
min(x[vyber]))/2
cista<-osum-o1
return(c(osum,cista))
}
Thanks again
Janusz Borkowski

        fit <- coxph(Surv(futime,event)~ 1, data=m)

Removing the 14 observations with expected 0 indeed solved for the GAM.

Feedback as reader "end-user" - I have a preference for the gam method 
described in the Poisson approach pages. So far it handles quite nicely 
huge data sets, with the bonus of confidence bands, and elegant test of 
the non-linear effects.

messages.subject: Re: logistic regression prediction
messages.body_plain:
Thank you everyone for useful responses to my question of Nov 07 2003:

In a multiple logistic regression, how does one find the standard error 
of the linear predictor used in generating confidence intervals around 
the predicted values? I am using glm() to perform logistic regression. 
Is there something analogous to the residual standard error produced by 
lm() for least squares regression?

Jim Stapleton (Michigan State University) provided the theoretical 
equations:

Let X be the design matrix. Let D be the n by n diagonal matrix of 
phat(1- phat) 's for the n   observations. Let B = X' D X. Then the 
approx. variances of the betahats are the diagonal terms of B-inverse.

Harry Southworth provided the Splus command line:
mypred <- predict(myglm, ci.fit=T)
will return an object with predicted values and 95% CIs on them.
With no further arguments, the returned predictions are on the scale of the
linear predictor.

Technical support at Insightful found some relevant comments on S-news, 
which pointed out that the predict function gives confidence intervals 
for the expected value but not for the predicted value for a future 
observation. Also, predict.glm, predict.lm have se.fit option, but 
predict.lme, predict mlm do NOT have an se.fit option.

Best regards,
Julia Reid

messages.subject: Re: optimization with linear constraints
messages.body_plain:
Include the adjustment in your derivative so that it is correct wrt to your 
adjusted objective.  Then the solver will "see" it.  This is known as 
reparameterization and is a common and effective technique -- it replaces a 
constrained optimization by a less constrained one.  The only tricky part 
here is to ensure that the sum of weights is > 0.  If it is possible to 
have all weights strictly greater than zero, then consider the transform w 
= exp(x) / sum(exp(x)), where x (a vector) is completely unconstrained, and 
w is a vector of positive weights that sums to 1.

hope this helps,

Tony Plate

CALL FOR PAPERS
     International Conference on Intelligent Agents, Web Technologies

                               12-14 July 2004

                             Gold Coast, Australia
       http://www.ise.canberra.edu.au/conferences/cimca04/index.htm

International Conference on Intelligent Agents, Web Technology and Internet

Commerce - IAWTIC'2004 provides a medium for researchers and practitioners 
to exchange

and explore the issues and opportunities in the area of intelligent agent, 
web technologies

and Internet commerce. The conference will consist of both plenary sessions 
and contributory

 sessions, focusing on theory, implementation and applications of 
intelligent agents,

 web technologies and Internet commerce.

Conference Topics Include (but not limited to):

Intelligent Agents
Knowledge Management
Intelligent Business Agents
Agent Architectures
Environments and Languages
Adaptation and learning for agents
Human and agent interaction
Interface agents
Mobile agents
Virtual agent-based marketplaces
Agents and uncertainty
The privacy issues for agents
Automated shopping and trading agents
Agent-oriented services
Social implications for agent
Conceptual modelling & Ontologies for agents
Agents and e-commerce
Legal aspects of agents in e-commerce
Performance measurement of e-commerce agents
Rational information agents and electronic commerce

Web Technologies
Web data mining and information retrieval
Agent-based trade-and mediating services
Teaching on Web
Virtual trading institutions
Knowledge Discovery
Intelligent Information Systems
Knowledge Clustering & Classification

Internet Commerce
E-commerce applications of Knowledge Representation
Reasoning Techniques
Electronic Payment Systems
Internet Marketing
Intranets and Extranets
Electronic Payment Systems
Electronic Data Interchange
Supply Chain Management
Electronic Payment Systems
Internet-based Electronic Commerce
Virtual Communities/Community Networks
Logistics Issues for Electronic Commerce
Business Reengineering Issues for Electronic Commerce
Government Electronic Procurement & Service Delivery
Legal & Security Issues for Electronic Commerce
Requirements Engineering for Electronic Commerce

PAPER SUBMISSION

Papers will be selected based on their originality, significance, 
correctness, and

clarity of presentation. Papers (4 pages or more) should be submitted

to the following e-mail or postal address:

E-mail submission of draft papers: iawtic at ise.canberra.edu.au
Postal Submission of draft papers: IAWTIC'2004 Secretariat
                                   School of Computing,
                                   University of Canberra,
                                   ACT, Canberra, 2614, Australia

Papers should present original work, which has not been published or

being reviewed for other conferences. Papers should be written in English. 
The name and

affiliation of authors should be omitted on the paper. A separate page must 
be included

 with each extended abstract paper, containing, the names, affiliations, 
postal address

and e-mail addresses of authors as well as the address of contact author. 
E-mail submission

of papers are encouraged.

Important Dates
· 14 March 2004 Submission of papers
· 30 April 2004 Notification of acceptance
· 21 May 2004 Deadline for camera-ready copies of accepted papers
· 12-14 July 2004 Conference sessions

Special Sessions and Tutorials
Special sessions and tutorials will be organised at the conference.
The conference is calling for special sessions and tutorial proposals.
All proposals should be sent to the conference chair on or before
 27th February 2004. CIMCA'04 will also include a special poster session
 devoted to recent work and work-in-progress. Abstracts are solicited
for this session. Abstracts (3 pages limit) may be submitted up to
30 days before the conference date.

Invited Sessions
Keynote speakers from academia and industry will be addressing the main
issues of the conference.

Visits and social events
Sightseeing visits will be arranged for the delegates and guests. A
separate program will be arranged for companions during the conference.

Further Information
For further information either contact iawtic at ise.canberra.edu.au
or see the conference homepage at:
http://www.ise.canberra.edu.au/conferences/iawtic04/index.htm

On Fri, 14 Nov 2003 19:39:55 -0500
Peng Huang <huangp at musc.edu> wrote:

> Prof. Harrell,

> Thank you! I tried lrm in Design library, but I don't understand

> 
> A<- data.frame(y = sample(1:3,50,T), race = sample(1:2,50,T),

> A$int<- A$race*A$gender
> x<- lrm(y~race+gender+int, data=A, na.action=na.delete,
>           method="lrm.fit")

First of all, take some time to understand the statistical modeling
language in S (e.g., look at Venables and Ripley and several other
sources).  You almost never create interaction terms yourself in S. 
Second, update the Hmisc and Design libraries (e.g., from
hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat/s/Hmisc.html).  Third, don't specify
default values for arguments.  Lastly, for categorical variables such as
race and gender the output will be more self-documenting if you make them
into factors with nice value labels.

Frank

messages.subject: lognormal distribution
messages.body_plain:
Dear list members,

I have collected data on minimum, maximum and median sizes (i.e. areas) of 
leaves in plant populations.

Using these three estimates, I would like to simulate frequency distributions 
of leaf sizes per plant with S-Plus, e.g.

-------------------------------

There are 50 leaves in total, mean area is 0.5, max area is 120, and median 
area is 64.
What would the total leaf area of the plant be, assuming that the leaf sizes 
are log-normally distributed? 

-------------------------------
To calculate this, I would need to simulate a standardized lognormal 
distribution based on the min, max and median values, and the total nr of 
leaves (which will give the nr of intervalls in the corresponding histogram) 

It would be great if anyone could help me with this question.

Best regards
Christoph.

-----------------------------------------------------

messages.subject: Re: lognormal distribution
messages.body_plain:
You want to be careful here.  You don't want to use just the min, max, and
median if you have more data than that.  After all, the minimum of a true
log-normal distribution is zero---you just didn't see any zeros in your
sample.  Also be careful if you take logs, then back transform into actual
areas, because you can create considerable bias that way.  See Parkhurst, D.
F. (1998). "Arithmetic versus geometric means for environmental
concentration data." Environmental Science and Technology 32(3): 92A-98A for
some relevant information.
It's not clear to me how you would use a fitted log-normal distribution to
get total leaf area.  One way might be:

Get the mean and variance of the logs of the data.  These are the parameters
of your log-normal distribution.

Then use Finney's bias-corrected geometric mean to get the average leaf
area, and multiply that by the number of leaves per plant to get the total
area.  Do not fail to correct for the bias using his correction.  Actually,
as suggested by my paper referred to above, you would probably get very
nearly the same result by taking the *arithmetic* mean of your 50 leaf
areas, then multiply by the total number of leaves per plant.  This works
well (and is unbiased) even if the individual areas are consistent with a
log-normal distribution.

Finney's correction is described in Finney, D. J. (1941). "On the
distribution of a variate whose logarithm is normally distributed." Journal
of the Royal Statistical Society (supplement) 7: 155-161.

The easiest way to calculate that correction is with a certain Bessel
function.  If you want more detail, let me know by private email.

Dave Parkhurst

messages.body_plain:
Greets all:

 

        I have a 
looping problem.  My loop contains a nested loop and there is lies the 
problem.

 

I have a nx2 matrix of coordinates(coormatrix), 
that identifies the center point of a sample strata, where the strata dimension 
is a user defined value.  The outside loop pulls the data from the 
coordinate matrix one point at a time (i.e. when i in the loop is equal the i th 
row in coormatrix).  A group of calculations is made on the coordinates and 
then sent to the inside loop.  Here I need the inside loop to perform a 
random sample for x and y, based on the calculations from the outside 
loop.  However, I may want more than one pair (x,y) of samples in each 
strata.  So, I set a sample number m, thus a mx2 matrix of samples.  
Finally, I would like to output these x,y pairs to a matrix with (nxm) rows and 
(2) columns - the result matrix .  

 

The adversary:

Say I set the number of samples to 3 (m=3), 
for i =1 in the outside loop there should be 3 x,y pairs; I would like 
these samples to fill the first 3 positions in the result matrix.  
For i =2 there should be another set of 3 samples, but they need to 
fill positions 4,5,6 in the result matrix.  There is the 
problem: how to get the interior loop to output values in a sequential and 
increasing order to the output matrix.

 

Below is the code I have developed so 
far.

#Strata Dimension

sadj_strata/2

#Result Matrix

mat3_matrix(0,length(n$x)*m,2)

#Outside Loop

for (i in 1:length(n$x)){

#Set x value

bx_n$x[n$nu==i]

#Set y value

by_n$y[n$nu==i]

#Set minimum x

bmnx_bx-sadj

#Set maximum x

bmxx_bx+sadj

#Set minium y

bmny_by-sadj

#Set maximum y

bmxy_by+sadj

#inside loop

for (j in 1:m){

# Random uniform sampling of x and y pair for each 
strata

mat3[j,1]_round(runif(1, min=bmnx, 
max=bmxx),5)

mat3[j,2]_round(runif(1, min=bmny, 
max=bmxy),5)

}

}

Currently, the first 3 positions of the result matrix is the only thing being 
filled, but it is being re-filled each time the entire loop is 
processed. 

Thanks in advance for any 
help!  
   

 

Best,
Dean Monroe
Oklahoma State 
University
Environmental Sciences

riyanto wibowo wrote:

> Dear S-Plus community,
>
>
>
> I have this function :
>
>
>
> function(a)
> {
>     for(a in a:100) {
>         if(a < 100)
>             rnorm(100 - a, a, a)
>         a <- a + 1
>     }
> }
>
> I want to make a function to generate (100-a) random number, with mean
> and standard deviation a; for 100-a times.
>
>
>
> But why when I use my own function, THERE IS NO OUTPUT AT ALL !!!.  Can
> somebody explain to me , what is my fault.

You're not returning anything from your function. Also, you are using 
the variable "a" dangerously. If you want to generate (100 - a) random 
variables (100 - a) times then use:

matrix(rnorm((100 - a)^2, a, a), nr = 100 - a, nc = 100 - a)

However, it's difficult to see exactly what you want and I may be off.

HTH,
Sundar

messages.subject: s-plus and c++ w/ borland
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am a bit unclear on using CONNECT/C++.  I've written a function in s-plus
(6.1 for windows) that randomly generates a set of spatial data, then
estimates the variogram using a method I've developed.  After a run, it
returns the estimated sill, range and nugget (from an nls fit).  What I
want to do is set up a "for" loop in a c++ program that repeatedly performs
the simulation and stores the estimates (doing so in s-plus is terribly
slow).  I've tried to use borland 5.0 to set up such a routine, however
I've encountered a myriad of problems (I'm not the most experienced c
programmer, but my hunch is that there is some discrepency between calling
conventions of borland and microsoft, but I'm probably wrong).  So my
question is, is it even possible to do this using borland?  If so, could I
see a simple example of calling an s-plus function in c++?  I've checked
the programming guide, and it was less than helpful, so I'd appreciate any
help.

Thanks

Isaac Grenfell
Fire Behavior Research
RMRS, Fire Sciences Lab
Missoula MT
igrenfell at fs.fed.us
406 829 6954

messages.subject: time-variant predictor in lme
messages.body_plain:
dear s-plus users,

a lme-model applied to a data-set of psychotherapy outpatients (unbalanced
longitudinal design, 1-5 assessments per patient during a two year period)
with
code = patient id,
sc10m = symptom outcome
in.studm = time since application for reimbursement (= baseline assessment)
status: i = in treatment (reference), k = no treatment during entire
obeservation time, n = after treatment, and v = before treatment

yields the following results

> summary(alle.t.lme)
Linear mixed-effects model fit by REML
 Data: alle
       AIC      BIC    logLik
  3177.703 3249.549 -1576.851

Random effects:
 Formula:  ~ in.studm | code
 Structure: General positive-definite
                StdDev   Corr
(Intercept) 0.48941237 (Inter
   in.studm 0.01150771 -0.232
   Residual 0.29130346

Fixed effects: sc10m ~ as.factor(status) * in.studm
                                Value  Std.Error   DF   t-value p-value
               (Intercept)  0.9305419 0.02370140 2225  39.26105  <.0001
        as.factor(status)k -0.0123474 0.06332289 2225  -0.19499  0.8454
        as.factor(status)n -0.1303128 0.04570860 2225  -2.85095  0.0044
        as.factor(status)v  0.1230537 0.02502128 2225   4.91796  <.0001
                  in.studm -0.0094344 0.00130486 2225  -7.23020  <.0001
as.factor(status)kin.studm  0.0003395 0.00298188 2225   0.11385  0.9094
as.factor(status)nin.studm  0.0045792 0.00237029 2225   1.93190  0.0535
as.factor(status)vin.studm -0.0184658 0.00955101 2225  -1.93339  0.0533

Standardized Within-Group Residuals:
       Min         Q1         Med        Q3     Max
 -4.235259 -0.4921071 -0.06625828 0.4164877 5.14915

Number of Observations: 2951
Number of Groups: 719

in order to keep all available data, i modeled status as a time-variant
predictor, i.e. for a given patient, usually a few measures were obtained
before, a few after, and most in-treatment, with large differences between
patients though, first of all because not all entered treatment, second,
start and duration of treatment differed markedly.
question: since i have a time-variant predictor, i am kind of lost when it
comes to interpreting findings in the summary output (intercept and slope),
e.g. intercept of observations after treatment which mostly lie around 1
year after 0 (time). more worries: i would like to include predictors, e.g.
baseline measures (SES, impairment level), but perhaps also predictive value
of in-treatment improvement and amount of treatment for post-treatment
outcome. but this is probably for later.

any help would be highly appreciated.

thanks

bernd

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

this is a very late reaction, for which i'm sorry, and i don't even know if it is ok for me to reply in this way, but something about this problem had made me a bit curious.

First of all thanks for your answer, it was very helpful and your solution was sufficient in most of the cases i had to examine. But still, when the two polynomials of which their quotient i want to fit get larger, eventually i still received the singular gradient matrix error. I understand that that can happen, that because of the overparameterization some parameters are dependent and the iterative process does not have a unique direction in which to look.
Instead of chosing one direction arbitrarily, it gives up.

My question is, why does it not choose an arbitrary direction? 
I have also formulated my regression model in the software program Stata (Sorry, i don't know if i'm cursing here?) and nothing's going wrong here. I don't know if the solution i receive really is the optimum but at least i've got án approximation. Or am i totally missing the point here?

Maybe you can explain this to me?

Greetings,

Joost van de Ven

>your model because the estimates are not unique. Multiply all the a's 

>by 2 and all the b's by 2 and you get the same fit. You can fit it if 

>you make one of the polynomials monic or you do something like 

> 

>T ~ cbind(1,h1,h2,h1*h2)/(1+b1*h1+b2*h2+b3*h1*h2), alg = "plinear" 

> 

>and optimize over only three parameters b1, b2, and b3. 

> 

>As Bert pointed out in private mail to me, problems of this nature 

>often arise from an overparameterized model. You are fitting 7 

>parameters to the data so you should be able to describe 7 different 

>characteristics of the data that will determine these parameters. It 

>may be difficult to do so. 

> 

>A common example of overparameterization is attempting to fit a 

>growth-curve model, like the four-parameter logistic, to (x,y) data that 

>cover only the initial part or only the terminal part of the curve. 

>Without data on both the "toe" and the "shoulders" of such a curve you 

>cannot fit four distinct parameters with any degree of precision.

messages.subject: Re: singular gradient matrix
messages.body_plain:
Spencer Graves <spencer.graves at pdf.com> writes:

>       I forget your earlier post.  Could you please remind us what
> function you are using?  From your description, I would guess it may
> be "nls".  Have you tried "optim(..., hessian=T)" in the MASS library?
> That seems to continue even when the gradient is singular.     hope
> this helps.  spencer graves

Do you perhaps have an overparameterized model?  Are you taking into
account the fact that one of the coefficients in either the numerator
or the denominator of a rational function must be set to a constant,
usually one?  If you don't do that then you can multiply all the
coefficients in the numerator by a constant and all the coefficients
in the denominator by the same constant and get the same prediction.
That is the symptom of a singular gradient matrix.

I am getting a surprising lack of fit in a loess plot and wanted to see

variables peragr8 and bttts4 (see attached scatter-bttt-perag-loess.sgr).
Plots between bttts4 and other variables also produce a poor fit (e.g.

I'm sorry, i thought the earlier posts were attached to this reply, but from your reaction i can see you could not read them. 

My problem finds its origin in heat management. I have a dataset with a temperature as output variable and quantifications of the external environment as inputs. I'm trying to fit a non linear regression model with nls, consisting of a quotient of two polynomials (of which one has to be monic indeed).

An example of such a model is:

T~(a0+a1*h1+a2*h2+a3*h1*h2)/(1+b1*h1+b2*h2+b3*h1*h2), where a's and b's are parameters, and h1 and h2 the inputs (heat transfer coefficients).

The model can be overparameterized indeed, because when i have more quantifications the fraction gets far more complex and i have to take some of the real parameters (which are the conductances in a network) together, and use the parameters a and b instead. 

This obviously is the reason that i receive the error message. Using the plinear-algorithm improves the results but in fact only postpones the problem. When the fraction models get to large, the estimation process doesn't converge anymore.

Using Stata, this is not the case. I am wondering what could be the reason for that. Is it that Splus does not want to give a solution of which it is absolutely not sure it even approximates an optimum? 

Maybe you can enlighten me.

Greetings,

Joost van de Ven

> plinear-algorithm?improves the results but in fact only postpones the
> problem. When the fraction models get to large,?the?estimation
> process?doesn't?converge anymore.
> 
> Using Stata, this is not the case. I am wondering what?could be the
> reason for that. Is it that Splus does not want to give a solution
> of which it is absolutely not sure it even approximates an optimum?

Yes.  The convergence criterion used by nls in S-PLUS and R is an
absolute criterion and not a relative criterion.  A study comparing
several popular statistics and econometrics programs on nonlinear
least squares examples (Spencer: Do you remember the reference?  It
was McCullough in American Statistician, wasn't it?) found that S-PLUS
and Shazam were the only two systems studied that this not declare
convergence to false optima at least once.  In the case of S-PLUS this
is because of the form of the convergence criterion.

Determining convergence of a nonlinear optimization algorithm is not
easy and is an aspect of algorithm design that is frequently
overlooked.  Declaring convergence to an optimum using a relative
change criterion doesn't mean that the algorithm has converged.  It
just means that the algorithm is no longer making progress.

messages.subject: Re: singular gradient matrix
messages.body_plain:
Doug mentioned an article that discussed nonlinear regression 
procedures finding false optima.  I believe the article was one of the 
following two:  

McCullough, B. D. (1999)
Assessing the reliability of statistical software: Part II
The American Statistician, 53, 149-159

McCullough, B. D. (1998)
Assessing the reliability of statistical software: Part I
The American Statistician, 52, 358-366

     McCullough also said that he used nlminb to find the optimum and 
then used those numbers as starting values for nls to get confidence 
intervals, etc.  Recently, Sundar Dorai-Raj and I have been using 
"optim(..., hessian=T)" to maximize a specialized likelihood or 
quasi-likelihood.  When the hessian becomes singular or nearly singular, 
we reduce the dimensionality and continue iterating.  This seems to have 
worked well as far as I know, but Sundar has more experience with it 
than I. 
     hope this helps.  spencer graves

messages.subject: New survival library
messages.body_plain:
A new set of functions that significantly expands the survival library
has been posted on our web site at Mayo.  Go to the web site for our
division  http://www.mayo.edu/hsr/biostat.html and you will find the
kinship library in the section on S-Plus functions.

  There are 3 major parts 
        
     coxme: a function for fitting general mixed-effects Cox models.
            This significantly expands the simple random effects (or
            frailty) models available by using the frailty() argument
            in coxph.

     functions for family data: creation and manipulation of pedigrees,
                                kinship matrices, and IBD matrices.  
     
     bdsmatrix: a class of objects for block-diagonal-sparse matrices.
                These are used in support of the above.

The motivating data set for much of the code is a large breast cancer
study with 26050 subjects in 426 families.  But coxme also been used for
simple shared frailty models, random treatment effects within site, 
and exploration of genetic linkage. The web page includes a draft technical
report with much more detail.

Locally, the most used function in the whole suite has been plot.pedigree.
This was a bit of a surprise, as the original goal of the function was to
support our debugging efforts for coxme.  It creates a very compact view,
usually arranged pretty well, automatically; but it is not an "artistic" 
competitor to established programs.  However, the ability to plot all the
pedigrees for a study in a simple for loop, along with simple annotations
with text() and title(), has made it quite popular.

        Terry Therneau
        Beth Atkinson
        Mayo Clinic College of Medicine

messages.subject: linear mixed integer programming problem
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I need to solve the following problem:

I have 10 sets of objects, say, A1, A2, ... , A10. They are not mutually exclusive. I need to pick up a set of subjects, say, B, such that the intersect of B and Ai (i=1,2,...,10) has at least ci (i=1,2,...,10) objects, where ci are fixed numbers. Note that the total number of objects is in thousands. 

I am trying to solve the problem using NUOPT. I set up my problem as follows:

X = (x1,x2, ... , xn) is 1xn {0,1}-vector

A = (aij) is nx10 {0,1}-matrix

minimize x1+x2+ ... + xn 

subject to 

  X*A >= C, or

  x1*a11+x2*a21+ ... +xn*an1 >= c1

  x1*a12+x2*a22+ ... +xn*an2 >= c2

  ...

  x1*a1,10+x2*a2,10+ ... +xn*an,10 >= c10

In NUOPT User's Guide, it says "MILP is very difficult class of problems. It may take hours to compute optimal solution of MILP with several hundred of integer variables." In my case, I have several thousands. Is there a practical solution for it? 

What are the options to solve this kind of problem in Splus?

Thank you very much!

results on the use of principled methods for reasoning under
uncertainty within intelligent systems. The scope of UAI is wide,
including, but not limited to, representation, automated reasoning,
learning, decision making and knowledge acquisition under
uncertainty. We encourage submissions that report on advances in these
core areas as well as submissions describing interesting and novel
systems that utilize techniques from these core areas.

The UAI 2004 conference will be held in Banff, Canada. The main
technical session will be on July 9-11, and will be preceded with an
advanced tutorial program on July 8th. The conference is collocated
with and follows both the Computational Learning Theory (COLT)
conference, which will be held July 1 through July 4, and the
International Conference on Machine learning (ICML), which will be
held July 4 through July 8. UAI 2004 coincides with the Calgary
Stampede Days, so we advise attendees to book flights, hotels, and car
rentals as early as possible.

Paper Submission: 
*****************

We encourage submissions that report on theoretical or methodological
advances in representation, automated reasoning, learning, decision
making and knowledge acquisition under uncertainty. We also encourage
submissions that report on systems that utilize techniques from these
core areas. Submitted papers will be carefully evaluated on the basis
of originality, significance, technical soundness, and clarity of
exposition. Papers submitted for review should represent original,
previously unpublished work. At the time the full paper is submitted
to UAI-2004, and for the entire review period, the paper should not be
under review by any other conference or scientific journal.

UAI-2004 requires electronic submission of papers and abstracts
according to instructions posted at the conference home page. If
authors have special circumstances that prevent electronic submission,
arrangements can be made directly with the program co-chairs listed
below. Authors are required to submit a title and a short abstract a
week before the paper submission deadline. Submitted papers must be
prepared according to the UAI-2004 proceedings format and must be no
more than eight (8) pages long, including figures and bibliography.
Papers that deviate from these guidelines will be rejected without
review. The conference home page will contain format information and
provides access to style files and templates.

Papers may be accepted for presentation in plenary or poster sessions.
All accepted papers will be included in the Proceedings of the
Twentieth Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence. The
program committee will select papers for special distinction in two
categories at UAI-2004: a "Best Paper" award, and an "Outstanding
Student Paper" award. The conference home page will contain
instructions for certifying student status with regards to the latter
award.

Key Dates: 
**********

Tuesday February 17, 2004, noon PST: Full paper submission

Thursday April 8, 2004, noon PST: Author notification of accepted papers
Thursday April 29, 2004, noon PST: Camera ready copy of accepted papers

These deadlines will be strictly enforced (but may change slightly!).

Please direct general inquiries to the General Conference Chair at
meek at microsoft.com. Inquiries about the conference program and
submission requirements should be directed to the Program Co-Chairs at
uai04-pchairs at cs.cornell.edu.

messages.subject: Re: sub-matrix and sub-data.frame
messages.body_plain:
If I understand your question, it is really about taking subsets of a
factor; the fact that the factors are "columns" of a data frame is
incidental.

Think of a factor as a representation of data assuming levels drawn from a
fixed set.  The fact that one of the levels doesn't happen to be
represented in the data at hand doesn't change the fact that the domain of
the data is that set of levels.  For example, human sexes are "male",
"female" -- if you pick a subset of a group of a people and all of them
happen to be men, you wouldn't immediately proceed to change the coding of
the "sex" variable.  This default treatment means you can take subsets of
the data and it will still be interpreted consistently with the original
coding (for example, if you fit a model and want ot make a prediction to a
new dataset).

There is an easy way to reduce the levels, which is to change the data to
character and then back to factor (which loses the information about the
original levels that are not in the data at hand).  Not a good default,
though.

        Alan Zaslavsky

On 21 Nov 2003, Ping Zhang wrote:
> If x is a data.frame that contains a factor column, then the
> corresponding "sub data.frame" seems to retain all the levels of the
> original data frame. This will not happen if I convert factors to
> characters first. This has given me troubles in more than one occasions.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ryan!

 

It looks to me like you have defined xbar, ybar and 
zbar to be

matrices, but each has only one column and one 
row.  In the loop

that gives the error message, you are trying to 
assign values 

to a matrix that has only one location but you are 
allowing 

i to loop over 1:data.

 

It sounds like you may have wanted to define larger 
matrices

to begin with.  (Splus doesn't grow them 
automatically if you

specify a location beyond the end.)  Also, 
though you can

assign values to the matrix using only one index 
(ie xbar[i]),

in that case Splus stacks the columns and counts 
through

them to find the ith element.  That may not be 
what you want.

 

Pete

Preliminary Call for Papers

ECML/PKDD-2004
Pisa, Italy, September 20-24, 2004
http://ecmlpkdd.isti.cnr.it
ecmlpkdd at isti.cnr.it

The 15th European Conference on Machine Learning (ECML) and the 8th European 
Conference 
on Principles and Practice of Knowledge Discovery in Databases (PKDD) will be 
co-located 
in Pisa, Italy, September 20-24, 2004. The combined event will comprise 
presentations of 
contributed papers and invited speakers, a wide program of workshops and 
tutorials, 
a demo session, and a discovery challenge.

Important dates 

- Submission deadline: Monday April 19, 2004 
- Notification of acceptance: Monday June 7, 2004
- Camera-ready copies due: Monday June 28, 2004

Paper submission 

High quality research contributions pertinent to any aspects of machine 
learning and 
knowledge discovery are called for, ranging from principles to practice; 
particular 
attention will be paid to papers describing innovative, challenging  
applications. 

There will be a single electronic submission procedure, where authors should 
indicate 
whether they submit their paper to ECML, PKDD, or both. In the latter case, the 
topic 
of the joint submission must be within the scope of both conferences; accepted 
joint 
submissions will be assigned to the most appropriate of the conferences. 
Student 
submissions should be clearly indicated on the submission form. All submissions 
will

Springer-Verlag

learning, automated 
scientific discovery, artificial intelligence, visualization, and high 
performance computing. KDD 
focuses on the value that is added by the creative combination of the 
contributing areas.

intends to provide an international forum for the discussion of the latest high

Dear Stefano,

At 12:24 PM 11/24/2003 +0000, Stefano Sofia wrote:
> Sorry for the trivial question:
> given a vector of numbers, which is the easiest way to determine the position
> of the maximum value within the vector?
> I have been looking in the manuals and in other books, with no success.

which(x == max(x)) gives you the index of the maximum (or indices if there 
are several maxima).

[In R, but not, I believe, in S-PLUS, there is also which.max(), which 
gives the *first* maximum (if there is more than one).]

I hope that this helps,
 John

messages.body_plain:
Dear list members: 

 

 If I have two normal distributions PD1(u1, s1) and PD2 (u2, s2), does SPlus have a function that will find the intersection point(s) of these two distributions with the two means and standard deviations as the input? (By this I mean the intersection point(s) as seen on a density plot of these two curves.) We can exclude the trivial situation where the curves are the same i.e. u1=u2, and s1=s2, in which case the two curves will be coincident upon each other and will intersect at all points.

 

On a related note, I have a column of data which when graphed in SPlus using a density plot produces a bimodal distribution, with two peaks and a local minimum in between. The curve then tails away to plus and minus infinity on right and left side respectively. Is there an elegant and efficent way of finding the exact position of the local minimum between the two modes using only the column of data points? ie I do not have any other information such as the equation of the curve etc...

 

Thanks for any help.

Lina

s1) - dnorm(x, m2, s2)
}

findintersect <- function(m1, s1, m2, s2) {
  lower 
<- min(m1 - 2*s1, m2 - 2*s2)
  upper <- max(m1 + 2*s1, m2 + 
2*s2)
  uniroot(twonorm, interval=c(lower, 
upper),
          m1=m1, s1=s1, 
m2=m2, s2=s2)
}

 

findintersect(1, 3, 4, 
2)

You 
may need to be careful with the situation where the two normals are far apart, 
so that the difference in the "middle" is too close to 0 for a large 
interval.

 

HTH,

Andy

messages.body_plain:
One can use the drop=T argument for factor subsetting to drop unused factor 
levels:

> x <- data.frame(a=letters[1:6],i=1:6)
>
> x1 <- x[1:2,]
> levels(x1$a)
[1] "a" "b" "c" "d" "e" "f"
> # drop unused levels in one column of a dataframe
> x1$a <- x1$a[,drop=T]
> levels(x1$a)
[1] "a" "b"
>

> # drop unused levels of all factor columns in a dataframe

> x1 <- as.data.frame(lapply(x[1:2,], function(col) if (is.factor(col)) 
col[,drop=T] else col))

> x1

  a i

1 a 1

2 b 2

> levels(x1$a)

[1] "a" "b"

>

-- Tony Plate

At Friday 09:26 PM 11/21/2003 -0500, Alan Zaslavsky wrote:
> If I understand your question, it is really about taking subsets of a
> factor; the fact that the factors are "columns" of a data frame is
> incidental.
>
> Think of a factor as a representation of data assuming levels drawn from a
> fixed set.  The fact that one of the levels doesn't happen to be
> represented in the data at hand doesn't change the fact that the domain of
> the data is that set of levels.  For example, human sexes are "male",
> "female" -- if you pick a subset of a group of a people and all of them
> happen to be men, you wouldn't immediately proceed to change the coding of
> the "sex" variable.  This default treatment means you can take subsets of
> the data and it will still be interpreted consistently with the original
> coding (for example, if you fit a model and want ot make a prediction to a
> new dataset).
>
> There is an easy way to reduce the levels, which is to change the data to
> character and then back to factor (which loses the information about the
> original levels that are not in the data at hand).  Not a good default,
> though.
>
>         Alan Zaslavsky
>
>
>

messages.body_plain:
>>Original question:
>>given a vector of numbers, which is the easiest way to determine the position
>>of the maximum value within the vector?
>
>Thanks to James Holtman, Fowler, Mark Fowler, Partha Bagchi, John Fox, Roula
>Tsonaka, Patrick Burns, Gerrit Eichner, Alan Dorfman and Tim Hesterberg for
>the quick replies.
>
>which(x == max(x)) is the easiest way, but not the only one.
>
>Unfortunately I forgot to tell you that I am using an obsolete version of
>Splus, Splus4, where the command which is not available. 
>I believe Gerrit Eichnerâ's hint is one of the best alternative solutions: 
>
>order(x)[length(x)]

order(x) requires O(n log(n)) time in general.  That solution
will be slow for large n.

I've tested a number of ways to do this, and think the
following is fastest all-around:
        first.max <- function(x) match(max(x,na.rm=T),x)
        first.min <- function(x) match(min(x,na.rm=T),x)

Tim Hesterberg

messages.subject: Multivariate Chart
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-news community,

I have function below (you can copy and paste it to your S-Plus,use fix(x)):

function(data, variable)
{
#PEMBANGUNAN T-SQUARE TAHAP YANG PERTAMA
 rerata <- matrix(0, data, variable)
 varian <- array(0, dim = c(variable, variable, data))
 M.covar <- matrix(0, variable, variable)
 selisih <- matrix(0, variable, data)
 Tsquare <- matrix(0, 1, data)
 for(i in 1:data) {
  acak <- matrix(rmvnorm(5, mean = c(10, 10, 10), sd = c(1, 1, 1)), ncol = variable)
  dimnames(acak) <- list(paste("Pengambilan ke-", 1:5), paste("Variable", LETTERS[24:26]))
  print(paste("BILANGAN ACAK KE :", i), quote = F)
  print(acak)
  for(j in i:i) {
   rerata[j, 1:variable] <- cbind(c(mean(acak[1:5]), mean(acak[6:10]), mean(acak[11:15]))
    )
   dimnames(rerata) <- list(paste("", 1:data), paste(LETTERS[24:26], "-BAR "))
   print(paste("RERATA DARI SAMPLE KE:"
 , i),
 quote = F)
   print(rerata[j, 1:variable])
   varian[1:variable, 1:variable, j] <- (var(acak))
   dimnames(varian) <- list(paste("Variable", LETTERS[24:26]), paste("Variable", LETTERS[
    24:26]), paste("Sample ke-", rep(j, data)))
   print(paste("MATRIX COVARIANCE UNTUK SAMPLE KE :", i), quote = F)
   print(varian[1:variable, 1:variable, j])
   M.covar[1:variable, 1:variable] <- M.covar[1:variable, 1:variable] + varian[1:variable,
    1:variable, j]
   for(aku in 1:2)
    print("", quote = F, digits = 1)
  }
 }
 print("SUMMARY:", quote = F)
 rerata2 <- matrix(c(mean(rerata[1:data, 1]), mean(rerata[1:data, 2]), mean(rerata[1:data, 3])), ncol
   = 1)
 dimnames(rerata2) <- list(paste("Variable", LETTERS[24:26]),
 paste("GRAND AVERAGE"))
 print(rerata2)
 s.pooled <- M.covar[1:variable, 1:variable]/data
 dimnames(s.pooled) <- list(paste("Variable", LETTERS[24:26]), paste("Variable", LETTERS[24:26]))
 print("MATRIX COVARIANCE (S-BAR)", quote = F)
 print(s.pooled)
 print("INVERSE DARI MATRIX COVARIANCE", quote = F)
 inverse <- solve(s.pooled)
 dimnames(inverse) <- list(paste("Variable", LETTERS[24:26]), paste("Variable", LETTERS[24:26]))
 print(inverse)
 for(k in 1:data) {
  selisih[1:variable, k] <- t(rerata[k, 1:variable]) - rerata2[1:variable, 1]
  Tsquare[k] <- 5 * (t(selisih[1:variable, k]) %*% (inverse %*% ((selisih[1:variable, k]))))
  dimnames(Tsquare) <- list(paste("T Square"), paste("Sample ke-", 1:data))
  if(Tsquare[k] > 7.75) {
   print(k)
  }
 }
 Tsquare
}

Once again, I apologize that the comment and the variable name is not written in English.  However you can still use the function above.  

As you know, that the function above is to search Hotelling T2 for Multivariate control chart.  This is for my thesis.  My question is :"Is my function valid ?". Because I've tried to generate 50 sample, but there is still point(s) was above 7.75 (7.75 is the control limit for large sample,say above 40-you can get it from Hotelling formula and F table).

How come ? Since the standard deviation is 1 for each variable. According to me, it should be "VERY" in control.

Any suggestion ?

Thanks.

Best regard,

Ryan

Thank you very much. For the moment i'm still continuing using only nls, still fitting my model consisting of the quotient of two polynomials. As i mentioned it could well be that there are two many parameters in my model. Therefore i want to know which terms (which a's and b's in my example) i have to include and which not. >and then used those numbers as starting values for nls to get 

>confidence intervals, etc. Recently, Sundar Dorai-Raj and I have 

>been using "optim(..., hessian=T)" to maximize a specialized 

>likelihood or quasi-likelihood. When the hessian becomes singular 

>or nearly singular, we reduce the dimensionality and continue 

>iterating. This seems to have worked well as far as I know, but

>> 

>>Yes. The convergence criterion used by nls in S-PLUS and R is an 

>>absolute criterion and not a relative criterion. A study comparing 

>>several popular statistics and econometrics programs on nonlinear 

>>least squares examples (Spencer: Do you remember the reference? It 

>>was McCullough in American Statistician, wasn't it?) found that 

>>S-PLUS 

>>and Shazam were the only two systems studied that this not declare 

>>convergence to false optima at least once. In the case of S-PLUS 

>>this 

>>is because of the form of the convergence criterion. 

>> 

>>Determining convergence of a nonlinear optimization algorithm is 

>>not 

>>easy and is an aspect of algorithm design that is frequently 

>>overlooked. Declaring convergence to an optimum using a relative 

>>change criterion doesn't mean that the algorithm has converged. It

messages.body_plain:
If your function is a ratio of two polynomials, then by 
multiplying both sides of the equation, you can make a linear regression 
of it;  just the act of trying this might expose problems.  After this, 
"stepAIC" in library(MASS) would work.  Alternatively, "lm(..., 
singular.ok=T)" would work with the full, transformed model.  Then if 
you still wanted the noise model implied by "nls", you should have 
decent starting values, etc. 

     Does this make sense? 
     spencer graves

messages.subject: Summary: Intersection point(s) of two Gaussian distributions.
messages.subject_clean: Summary: Intersection point(s) of two Gaussian distributions.
messages.body_plain:
The original questions:

 

If I have two normal distributions PD1(u1, s1) and PD2 (u2, s2), does SPlus have a function that will find the intersection point(s) of these two distributions with the two means and standard deviations as the input? (By this I mean the intersection point(s) as seen on a density plot of these two curves.) We can exclude the trivial situation where the curves are the same i.e. u1=u2, and s1=s2, in which case the two curves will be coincident upon each other and will intersect at all points.

 

On a related note, I have a column of data which when graphed in SPlus using a density plot produces a bimodal distribution, with two peaks and a local minimum in between. The curve then tails away to plus and minus infinity on right and left side respectively. Is there an elegant and efficent way of finding the exact position of the local minimum between the two modes using only the column of data points? ie I do not have any other information such as the equation of the curve etc...

 

Thanks to Andy Liaw, Martin Maechler, Robert Byers, L. Molinari, and Bert Gunter for their suggestions.

 

For part one of the problem, the best consensus solution is to solve the resulting quadratic equation which results from subtracting one equation from the other and setting the result equal to zero. Bert Gunter was the first to suggest this approach and Robert Byers, L. Molinari and Martin Maechler  independently concurred. Andy Liaw presented a iterative solution using the SPlus uniroot function, which was quite useful to me, as I will be able to use this approach for other instances when an easy solution will not be possible.

 

There have been no implementable responses for the second part, except from Bert Gunter, who suggested consulting a professional statistician who may be able to solve the problem using the EM algorithim. He thinks that this is a mixtures distribution problem (mixed effects?)

 

Once again, thanks to all who responded. I very much appreciate your help and timely responses.

 
Lina

messages.body_plain:
I do this kind of thing all the time, but using get( ) in a for( ) loop is
not the way I do it.  I don't think that would achieve anything in my case.

With only 20 steps to the loop it becomes feasible to do it one step at a
time, if all you need to do to acomplish a step is is just press F10 or
click the "go" arrow (alternatively, in unix/linux, press the uparrow and
return).

The knack is pretty simple but difficult to describe in detail.  It relies
on using substitute( ) and eval( ), so you need to construct what would be
the body of the loop as a language object and modify it by inserting the
name of the object each time as part of the the loop operation.  The other
thing is that you need to use "substitute" indirectly, so that means a
do.call(), which is always fun.  

Let me give an example.  The objects I deal with are named B1970, B1971,
..., B2003, say, and each is huge.  Each is a data frame and suppose I want
to run a function fun(...) on each and collect the results in a list, with
the appropriate names.

Assuming windows and using a script file, the initialisation part goes as
follows:

xxxx <- 1970
res <- list()
expr <- Quote({
        res[[as.character(xxxx)]] <- fun(Bxxxx)
        print(xxxx <- xxxx + 1)
})

Now the loop part, which is the tricky bit.

eval(do.call("substitute", list(expr,
                list(Bxxxx = as.name(paste("B", xxxx, sep = ""))))))

You evaluate the initialisation part first.  Then highlight the loop part
and repeatedly evaluate it by pressing f10, say.  The result will let you
know where you are up to using the print(....) part of the expr.  The way it
works is to evaluate the expression repeatedly with the name of the object
substituted each time as appropriate.  This can easily be adapted to cases
where the objects are not so regularly named, of course.

What we are doing, of course, is making manual evaluation of the loop as
simple as possible in order to control the overhead due to backout, but
losing backout is the price you pay for it.

More stuff in S Programming, if anyone wants more.

Bill Venables.

messages.subject: Re: Looping over objects
messages.body_plain:
I often do this sort of thing, and sometimes use get(), in something like 
the following manner (where the objects named x1 ... x20 are my "sublists")

> results.summary <- lapply(1:20, function(i) {x <- 
get(paste("x",i,sep=""); return(some.summary.func(x))})

When memory usage becomes an issue I consult things like the section on 
memory usage in the Programmer's Guide, and the documentation for arguments 
such as immediate= in the get() function.

When I need to make keeping track of what's what more convenient, I use a 
function like:

> named.obj <- function(names., x=names.) {names(x) <- names.; x}

and do:

> results.summary <- lapply(named.obj(paste("x",1:20,sep="")), 
function(obj.name) some.summary.func(get(obj.name)))

(which is the same as the above, except that the list of results is named 
with the names of the respective objects)

If I need to save results from each object in individual objects, I use the 
assign() function (with argument where=1).

hope this helps,

Tony Plate

messages.body_plain:
Have you considered keeping the master copy of your function in 
another word processor or text editor, formatted as you like it, then 
copying it into an S-Plus script file each time you want to use it?  If 
your thesis is in MS Word, you could keep the function in Word.  I don't 
know Emacs, but a friend uses ESS (Emacs Speaks Statistics;   
http://www.analytics.washington.edu/Zope/wikis/ess/) for both S-Plus and 
R.

Biostatistician 
I am assisting to recruit a Biostatistician for an academic 
research group located in Boston, MA. 
Below is more information on this opportunity. Thank you so much - have a 
wonderful day, 

Khristine 

This client is seeking a highly-qualified Biostatistician to support all 
aspects of clinical investigation, including design and analysis of clinical 
studies, collaborate with investigators affiliated with a major medical school, 
grant and protocol development and review, and teaching and mentoring of junior 
investigators. 

The individual must have:

*an M.S. or Ph.D. in statistics or Biostatistics

*a strong record of collaborative research

*3+ years experience

*excellent interpersonal skills

*excellent oral and written communication

*multitasking capability to handle numerous simultaneous projects

*a strong commitment to excellence in research. 

Candidates with broad consulting interests who enjoy collaborating with 
physicians and research staff are encouraged to apply. Expertise in study 
design, grant writing, clinical trials, case-control and cohort studies, 
statistical genetics, hierarchical, longitudinal, survival, nonlinear, SAS. 

The Biostatistician will have a research associate appointment. and not a 
clinical trials coordinating center. 

Interested candidates should send a letter of interest, CV, writing sample, 
and reference information to resumes at workwondersstaffing.net 

Senior Recruiter
Work Wonders Staffing
http://www.workwondersstaffing.net
